1:
The order is given openly, and that openness is what the commentators seize on. Gill explains the choice of confidant: the heir to the crown might be expected to see where his own interest lay, listen to a father rather than a friend, and turn against a rival, however much he had loved him. Henry calls it malice that was not even ashamed of itself, since the king proclaimed an outlaw and charged his household on their allegiance to kill him without being able to give a reason, and without apparently fearing that servants who all loved David might rebel at such an order. Henry's aside is that malice was either less politic then, or justice less corrupt, than later, or else the king would have had the man indicted on suborned testimony and killed by colour of law as Naboth was — and his comfort is that there is least danger from malice that does not disguise itself. He adds that a father who knew how well his son loved David can only have reckoned the heir as envious as himself, and that providence used the miscalculation to give David a protector. Clarke measures the danger the same way: with every officer about the king's person and every soldier under positive orders, nothing short of God's particular interposition could have saved the man's life. Ellicott prefers a stricter rendering, that Saul spoke of intending David's death, which is how the Greek and Syriac take it, and traces the impulse through three stages — first the spear grasped and poised in a paroxysm at the musician who was trying to calm him, then the schemes to send a young soldier into deadly enterprises, and now open talk to his heir and counsellors about the risk of letting so dangerous a man live.

Against that, the friendship. Gill describes a love of complacency, constant and steadfast, in the man's company and conversation, and notes the practical mercy in it, since this was how David came to know what was intended and could guard himself. Henry's version is warmer and sharper: a friend in need, who went on delighting in a man whose glory had eclipsed his own and who now stood up for him when the whole stream ran the other way. The first service was simply the warning, and Henry explains why it was needed, since Jonathan could not be sure that none of the servants was obsequious enough, or envious enough, to carry out the order if he came across David. Ellicott puts the same point as a political observation: a powerful king need only hint at wanting to be rid of an obnoxious subject for unscrupulous men to commit a murder they imagine will please him. Clarke suggests the execution may have been set for the following day, which is why the warning fixes on that morning and tells him to hide.

The plan for the interview is reported with some care about its timing. Gill has the son going out at the hour his father was accustomed to walk, and Ellicott takes the field for some garden or quiet place where the king habitually resorted with his friends and counsellors. Henry offers three reasons why nothing was attempted that night: the king was in drink and unfit to be spoken to, or a night's sleep might make him revoke the order himself, or there was simply no opportunity before morning. Keil and Delitzsch describe the attempt as a son pointing out, with all the modesty proper to a son and as earnestly as he could, the grievous wickedness of what his father was doing. Henry's judgement on the method is that it was prudent and managed with the meekness of wisdom, and that speaking well of a friend at the risk of a father's displeasure is a rare instance of friendship worth the name.
4:
What the plea contained is itemised differently by each voice. Gill lists the heads: a good man, good things done, wisdom and prudence in the management of his affairs, valour in his expeditions, and faithfulness to his king and country in every instance. Clarke draws the inference about the pleader rather than the plea, that Jonathan was plainly satisfied of David's innocence and of his father's being unjustly incensed. Ellicott dwells on who was speaking — the heir to the throne, the man most likely of all to be injured by the rising popularity of the soldier whose life was in question — and then turns the argument into direct speech, recalling the day the giant was fought and the pebble slung, when a hair's breadth of error would have left the champion dead and Israel undelivered. Wesley's whole comment is on the cost: it could not be done without hazard to the speaker, and in doing it he discharged the duty both of a true friend and of a valiant man.

The force of the reasoning is separately remarked on. Gill fastens on the phrase about putting a life in one's hand, taking it to mean a man exposing himself to the utmost danger when nobody else in the whole camp of Israel would do the like. Keil and Delitzsch set the clauses out in order, the risked life, the Philistine killed, the great salvation wrought by the Lord for all Israel, the king's own eyes that saw it and rejoiced, and then the question why he would sin against innocent blood and kill without cause. Clarke's estimate is that the pleading, short as it is, is exceedingly cogent, and the argument such as could not be resisted.

The oath is taken at face value by everyone who comments on it. Gill has the king not merely hear his son out but be affected and wrought upon, convicted for the time that he was wrong, with the Lord working on his mind to incline him. Ellicott makes the eloquence touch his heart, so that for a short while something of the old noble spirit governed him. Wesley has no doubt he meant what he swore, feeling a real change in himself for the present, and he quotes Henry's sentence that God inclined the heart of Saul to hearken to the voice of Jonathan. Clarke infers an administrative consequence that the text does not record, that orders contrary to the previous day's must have gone out. On the restoration itself Gill has the friend call David out of his hiding place in the field once the king had gone home, and Clarke notes that the man who had been hidden on the day appointed for his murder simply resumed his place at court on the strength of the oath. Both Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott end the paragraph by looking forward: the one observing that the reconciliation unfortunately did not last long, the other that the old life went on as before, with David received on terms of intimacy, until a fresh occasion lit the slumbering fires again.
8:
The campaign is small but the service is the point. Gill doubts either side committed its whole force, taking the fighting for skirmishes between detachments. Henry makes the renewed war an occasion for two loyalties: the sword used as boldly as ever, with a brave charge, many killed and the rest put to flight, and the harp taken up as cheerfully when the old fits of melancholy returned. On the harp he presses the moral twice, that a humble man counts nothing beneath him by which he may do good, and that a man nearly speared at that same employment the last time had learned to render good for evil and trust God with his safety. Wesley compresses the same thought, that those ill paid for doing good must not grow weary of it, remembering how bountiful a benefactor God is even to the evil and unthankful. Henry's opening observation is the sharper one: the very usefulness that should have earned gratitude was the thing envied, and David neither sulked nor withdrew from public service on that account.

The relapse is explained at three levels. Gill and Clarke keep to the man, a melancholy and frantic disorder returning on news of the victories, envy and jealousy producing distraction of mind, which Clarke says was exacerbated by diabolic influence; Wesley has the devil watching his opportunity as before. Henry puts the causation the other way round: indulged passion invited the evil spirit, since letting the sun go down on wrath gives the devil room, and disorders of mind, however much Satan furthers them, commonly begin in a man's own sins and follies. Keil and Delitzsch read the narrator's phrase as naming a higher cause, the attack inflicted by Jehovah, so that the growth of the king's melancholy marks the hardness of heart he had been given up to for his impenitence. Ellicott treats the phrase as the hard saying it is, notes that the Greek was offended enough to drop the divine name altogether, and argues that no expositor has fully explained it. His own position is cautious: scripture gives only scattered notices of the spirit world, and to make malignant beings part of the heavenly host is at variance with any proper conception of the All-Father, though one may grant that spirits fallen through sin remain God's even in their degradation and are sometimes permitted, for hidden reasons, to plague particular souls — as a trial of faith with Job, and as punishment for desertion of God here. Ellicott also quotes Browning's poem on Saul twice, contrasting the silence of this fit with the days when the musician's playing drew the king back into life.

The spear itself gets a note. Ellicott identifies it as the great spear that appears in scene after scene of this book, in the king's hand or at his side, and Henry sees a man made a torment to himself by fear, unable to sit at home without it, pretending defence while intending murder. Gill describes the aim, to strike through the body and pin it to the wall as before, and Henry marks the violence of the throw by where it landed. Henry adds a motive the text does not give: the king may have reckoned that a killing in such a state would be excused before God and man as the act of a man out of his mind, which is a pretence God cannot be deceived by. On the escape, Clarke credits bodily agility in a man who knew he could not trust the king and was continually on his watch, and Keil and Delitzsch have him slip aside so that the weapon struck the wall. Henry's reading is providential rather than athletic, a blow missed and a man preserved through that night, and he points to the Psalms where David calls God his shield and buckler, his rock and his fortress.
11:
The ambush at the door is reconstructed with some care. Gill has the messengers sent on the assumption that David had gone home, and places the house, which the text does not locate, probably at Gibeah where the king lived. Henry confirms the assumption was right, and reports Josephus for an alternative account of the intention, that David was to be seized and hurried before a court already instructed to condemn him as a traitor — against which Henry sets the plainer thing the text says, that the guards were simply to kill him. Clarke explains the choice of hour by the danger of the dark: in the night they could not have distinguished husband from wife, and the king, who wished the man represented as a traitor, could hold an attack justifiable at any hour, full daylight included. Henry turns to the psalm David wrote on this occasion, where the watchers at the house are complained of as bloody men with swords in their lips.

The deliverance comes through the wife, and Henry makes the most of the irony. She had been given to David as a snare and proved his protector instead, which is how the devil is often out-shot with his own bow. How she learned of the danger he cannot say, guessing either at notice sent from court or at her own eye on the soldiers settling round the house as the household went to bed, quiet enough that the psalm can ask who hears them. Knowing her father's temper she suspected the design at once and set about saving her husband. Her warning Henry renders in Josephus's words, that if the sun saw him there next morning it would never see him again. He adds a soldier's observation, that David was better versed in fighting than in flying and could easily have cleared the house with the sword had that been lawful, and that the window was used because every door was watched. Ellicott reads her decision as a judgement about her father: the veil had now been publicly lifted from his design, and she knew there was no hope for her husband but instant flight.

The escape itself is recorded plainly, and three of them add something to it. Gill supplies two parallels, the spies let down from a house in Jericho while the king's men searched for them, and the apostle let down at Damascus out of the reach of those who waited for him. Clarke works out the geography: the watchers would naturally hold the gate or lie in wait wherever David must come out, so the letting down was probably at the back of the house, where there was neither door nor way through, and the ambush was eluded without being passed. Keil and Delitzsch report the window, the going, the flight and the escape without comment, as the narrative gives them. Henry's interest is in what David did next, since the psalm belongs either to the closet before he went or to the hiding place he fled to, and either way it shows a mind composed in the middle of fright and hurry, with faith fixed on God. He makes the point sharpest by the hour named on each side: the plot was to kill him in the morning, and the psalm undertakes to sing aloud of mercy in the morning. Ellicott closes on the length of what was beginning, since with this desperate flight began the weary wanderings and the perpetual risks that ran on until the king's death released him.
13:
The thing laid in the bed has a name that puzzles them all. Gill transliterates rather than translates it, notes that if these were the objects Rachel stole they belong with the household gods of the heathen, and infers they were kept privately, since David would not have allowed them indoors. He then stacks up the Jewish explanations: Aben Ezra's, that they were figures cast under a constellation to draw heavenly influences and foretold things when consulted; and one rabbi's, that Michal laid them there so her father would suppose David had found them and know why he fled. Gill answers the second himself: consulting such images was far from David, who needed no help to know what the king intended. Clarke keeps to what the scene requires: the word covers any image standing for some reality, and this one must have been in human form, to pass for a man lying ill in bed. Ellicott adds grammar and history — a plural form used as a singular, with no singular on record, matched oddly by the Latin word for household gods, also only plural — and reads the class as a relic of the idolatry some of Abraham's family brought from Chaldaea, looked on as tutelary deities and dispensers of domestic good fortune. He notes they ranged from the small figure Rachel hid under a camel saddle to the life-size one needed here, and repeats the suggestion that this princess kept hers secret because of her barrenness.

The dressing of the figure is read two ways. Clarke takes the goats' hair for a pillow or bag muffling a sick man's head, and calls the material accidental unless it was meant for David's own hair, which he thinks not improbable. Ellicott renders it a goat's skin set about the head, with the Syriac and Latin behind him, for that same purpose, and reports the alternative that it was a net of goats' hair to keep flies off the supposed sleeper. He also explains how Josephus came to describe a palpitating goat's liver in the bed: the Greek read liver where the Hebrew has skin, a confusion easy before the vowel points and between two letters that differ slightly. Wesley agrees the hair went on the head and face to give some resemblance in a sick man's room, where there is usually only a glimmering light, and takes the covering as part of the pretence. Ellicott identifies the cloth as David's everyday garment, which thrown loosely over the image would help the deception. On the psalm assigned to this night the two part company: Clarke supposes it was written then, while Ellicott, granting the song is David's and the danger probably in his mind, finds the internal evidence scarcely confirming the title, since some references must belong to other passages of his life.

The second embassy breaks the deception. Gill offers two accounts, either the same men returning or fresh ones sent because the first stayed longer than expected and were suspected of negligence; and the order to see David was not kindness, since they were to look at his person and settle whether he was sick and whether he was there, having before taken the wife's word without laying eyes on him. Keil and Delitzsch give the command to carry him up bed and all, the discovery of the image, the charge of deceit, and then weigh her answer. On their reading she pleads that she was obliged to yield to a threat on her life, representing herself as never having meant to let him go — a prevarication they think she considered perfectly justifiable. Clarke unpacks the sentence as a conditional with the threat implied, and excuses her: a wife satisfied of her husband's innocence could do no less than favour his escape. Gill places the interview after the messengers' report, at her house or at the palace.
18:
Where David ran is a choice, not an accident. Gill records only the escape from the house and from the men waiting in it. Henry notices what the fugitive did not do: he went neither to his relations at Bethlehem nor to any city that had lately cried him up, where he might have built an interest for his own preservation, but straight to the prophet with the whole story. Henry gives three reasons. The first is that this was the man who had given him assurance of the crown, so that a failing faith — a man in flight is ready to say that all men are liars, the one who promised his life and the one who promised him a throne alike — went where the assurance could be renewed, which Henry calls making God his refuge. The second is that a prophet was the best adviser in such a strait, with the rule drawn from it that those who expect answers of peace to their prayers must keep their ears open to God's word. The third is the company: a college of prophets to praise God with, and a man who found little rest in the king's court looked for it in the prophet's church. Clarke supposes he came for advice and that Samuel judged it best to keep him for the present where he had his school. Wesley adds safety to comfort and direction, on the reckoning that the king would be ashamed to do murder in the presence of so venerable a person. Ellicott measures the authority that implies, since the seer kept influence enough, even in the stormy close of the reign, for a frightened man to treat his quiet house of prayer and learning as a sanctuary, and describes the relation between them as that of a loved pupil.

The place itself needs explaining, and two of them explain it. Ellicott says it was no town but, as the name shows, a cluster of dwellings, from a verb meaning to rest or abide: the prophet's house was in Ramah and these abodes, where his schools were kept, stood in the immediate neighbourhood, which is why the text says Naioth in Ramah. He adds that the Chaldee paraphrase simply calls it a house of learning. Henry treats it as a privileged place as well as a lodging, since not even the Philistines would disturb that meeting.

How the king came to know is the hinge of the paragraph. Gill attributes it to officious persons who saw David at Ramah and marked that he and Samuel went off together, and Keil and Delitzsch have the king informed where the place was before he sent to fetch him. They pause on the grammar of what the messengers saw, where a singular verb stands oddly for a company: it is no copyist's slip, since such a slip would hardly have got into every manuscript, and they take it of the officer leading the party or of the party as one body. The rare word for the prophetic company they read, with the ancient versions, as an assembly, formed by simple inversion from a commoner word, as Kimchi and other rabbins held. Henry looks ahead and reads a man baffled by one providence after another without drawing the inference: officers sent, then more, then a third party, and at last the king himself, which Henry thinks beneath a king but no surprise in a persecutor, who will stoop to anything and drop all public business to gratify his malice. His figure for the deliverance is one David would have understood, a lamb at the mouth of the lions, saved neither by the lion's being killed, as the shepherd once saved his own lamb, nor by fire from heaven on the messengers, as a later prophet was, but by the lions being turned for the time into lambs.
20:
Gill's first remark is on the effrontery of the attempt, a king sending officers into a sacred place because he was so bent on the man's destruction. What they walked in on is described in careful terms. Clarke has the company engaged in religious exercises with Samuel as head or president of the school there, and Ellicott notes that the word rendered company occurs nowhere else in scripture, though the ancient versions agree on company or assembly, the Chaldee paraphrasing it as a company of scribes praising while Samuel stood over them teaching. Wesley makes most of the presiding. Inspiration did not excuse preparation, on his account, since those who prophesied had both to make themselves ready beforehand and to turn the gift to good use afterwards, and needed counsel for either; a presiding prophet was also the safeguard against pretended raptures and against a devil transforming himself into an angel of light; and Samuel's joining the exercises encouraged the company and stirred up others to covet such gifts.

What then happened to the officers is agreed to be outside ordinary experience. Ellicott says so plainly, and holds that the only possible explanation is the clause immediately before it, that the Spirit of God came upon these men. He then borrows Ewald's reconstruction of the scene: men who arrived with hostile intentions stopping short, held by the music and the solemn dance, drawn further into the circle until they broke out in the same words and gestures, flung off their outer garments, joined the dance, and sank into an ecstasy that left them with no memory of what they had come for. Wesley reaches the same end by a different comparison, that they were inspired as Balaam was, and that the rapture took their minds wholly off the design of seizing David. Clarke puts it most briefly: they partook of the same influence and joined the same exercise, and so were prevented.

The repetition is what makes the point. Keil and Delitzsch record that a second company and then a third fared exactly as the first had, each sent after the news of the last reached the king, and Gill describes what that news was — messengers who, instead of making an arrest, were found at services of quite another kind than the one they were sent on. Ellicott closes with a use the Church made of the passage: he reports Bishop Wordsworth's note that the whole section from the flight to the end of the chapter, with the Spirit coming on the messengers and on the king who sent them, was appointed to be read on Whitsun Tuesday, as evidence that the Holy Spirit was at work before the times of the Gospel and that his agency is free and powerful; and he sets beside it the history of Eldad and Medad, read on the day before.
22:
The king goes himself only after the third party fails to come back, and Gill marks the route from Gibeah to Ramah. Keil and Delitzsch stop at the landmark on the way, a great pit or well at a place near Ramah which they admit is unknown to them, and have him ask there where the prophet and David were and go on according to the answer he got. Gill has him simply continue from the well toward the place. Clarke reads the seizure as beginning at that well, so that the whole remaining distance was covered in prophesying, which he glosses as praying and singing praises. Wesley makes the difference of place the point of the whole episode: the Spirit came on the king in the way, where it had not come on his messengers until they reached the spot, and the lesson intended was that his designs against David were vanity and that in them he was fighting against God.

The stripping and the word for nakedness are handled with some care by everyone. Keil and Delitzsch record the clothes taken off, the prophesying before Samuel, and the lying there a whole day and night, then note that the word does not always mean complete nudity but is used of a man with his upper garment off; they also observe that the repeated phrase about the king doing this too shows that he came into the same ecstatic condition as his servants. Gill limits it to the upper garments, as men in such circumstances and prophets themselves sometimes did, and as the messengers seem to have done, and he reports the Jewish view that the royal robes came off in exchange for the habit of the scholars and sons of the prophets. Clarke has the royal or military dress thrown off and the tunic kept, with the day and night spent in prayers, praises and other exercises unusual in kings and warriors. Ellicott adds the undergarment, since men of the upper ranks certainly wore a fine-woven shirt of linen or cotton beneath the tunic, and cites Lyranus for taking the phrase to mean no more than the outer robe laid aside. Wesley renders the posture more strongly, since the Hebrew has him fall to the earth, his mind in an ecstasy and his senses not at his command; and he reads the length of it as deliberate, God keeping the king as if in chains, with the day and night repeated to show how long, until David was out of reach.

What the outpouring meant divides them. Ellicott points out that it was not the first time, since the Spirit had come on this man among prophets at Gibeah just after his anointing, and had then made him another man altogether. He reports one explanation of the present case from the Chaldee, as Raschi takes it, that the king was simply mad, and prefers another: that the Spirit was pleading once more with the man the Lord had chosen to anoint, and that the pleading was forgotten as soon as the strange excitement passed — which Ellicott asks whether we do not see every day. Clarke's account is providential rather than psychological, that by bringing both the king and his men under a divine influence God kept them from touching David. On the proverb, Ellicott explains how it gained currency, the thing having happened once before, and why it struck people: there seemed something strange in a man so self-willed and disobedient receiving, as the bystanders saw it, the divine and much coveted gift. Wesley takes the revived proverb as evidence of God's care, in a sentence that turns on itself — the king was made a prophet in some sort so that David might be made a king.
